label: Title
notes: Open by framing the section as a calculus for convex objects, not a bag of isolated closure facts. The main promise is that sums, scalings, products, images, preimages, and hulls can be inspected by following convex combinations through the operation. Keep the closure caveat for later.

label: Minkowski Sum
notes: Emphasize that A plus B contains every point formed by adding one point from each set. Convexity of the sum is not mysterious: average two sums by averaging their A parts and B parts separately. The support check gives a numerical handle on the same rule.

label: Scalar Multiplication
notes: Treat scalar multiplication as a map first and a picture second. Positive scalars dilate, negative scalars reflect and dilate, and zero collapses everything to one point. Convexity survives because multiplying a convex average is the same as averaging the multiplied endpoints.

label: Weighted Sums
notes: The weighted-sum slide is the algebraic engine behind many later constructions. Show that nonnegative weights let us build new convex sets from old ones, and remind students that the special case of the same set returns the set itself rather than a larger object.

label: Products And Slices
notes: Use the product as the cleanest way to prove many rules at once. A product is convex because each coordinate can be averaged independently. A slice is convex because it is an intersection with an affine constraint, which keeps every segment satisfying the same constraint.

label: Affine Images
notes: The image rule is the forward transport rule. If students remember only one line, make it the equation saying affine maps commute with convex averages. Mention that images can reduce dimension, so preservation of convexity is not preservation of ambient shape.

label: Inverse Images
notes: The inverse-image rule is the feasibility rule. Rather than drawing a set directly, define it by the requirement that a mapped point lands in a convex target. The average of two feasible points maps to the average of their images, so feasibility survives.

label: Hull Commutation
notes: Present hull commutation as a finite certificate saver. We may first take all convex combinations and then map them, or map the generators and take combinations afterward. The coefficients do not change, which is why point-cloud checks are so reliable here.

label: Hulls And Sums
notes: Make the equality precise, because this is where students often undercount sums. Convex hulls commute with Minkowski sum only when the sum side contains all pairwise sums of generators. If we add only matched pairs, we usually get a smaller set.

label: Dimension Bookkeeping
notes: Pause for bookkeeping. Algebraic operations can preserve convexity while changing affine dimension, lineality, or direction space. This slide gives students a compact checklist: translation and nonzero scaling preserve dimension, products add, sums span combined directions, and linear maps are limited by rank.

label: Cones
notes: Cones are the homogeneous version of the story. Nonnegative scaling is built into their definition, so sums, linear images, preimages, and products stay conic. A translation is the useful warning: it can keep convexity but usually destroys the cone structure.

label: Closure Warning
notes: Use the epigraph example to separate convexity from closedness. The epigraph is closed and convex, but projecting it loses the limiting boundary value zero. This is the boundary behavior that makes closure hypotheses matter in set algebra.

label: Rules Ledger
notes: Read this slide like a ledger students can consult during proofs. Each row records the operation, the convexity argument, what can happen to dimension or closure, and the toy check behind the deck. It turns the lecture into a practical diagnostic table.

label: Recap
notes: Close with an inspection routine rather than a list of slogans. For any new operation, ask where the convex coefficients go, whether dimension changed, whether closure was silently assumed, and which finite or support-function check would catch a mistake.
